indexing.paragraph: Forecasting Bike Rental Demand Using Tree-Based Models

Bike-sharing systems such as Washington D.C.'s Capital Bikeshare require accurate demand forecasts to manage bike availability, storage, and relocation costs. Our goal is to predict the hourly count of bike rentals using historical rental data, weather conditions, and calendar information. The evaluation metric is Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE):

where pi​ is the predicted count, ai​ is the actual count, and n is the number of observations. Lower RMSLE indicates better predictions. RMSLE penalizes under-predictions more heavily than over-predictions, which is appropriate for demand forecasting where stockouts are costlier than surplus. The log transformation also handles the wide range of rental counts (1 to ~977 rentals/hour) without over-weighting high-count hours.
We used the Kaggle Bike Sharing Demand dataset, derived from the Capital Bikeshare program in Washington D.C. spanning 2011–2012.
Original features (12): datetime, season, holiday, workingday, weather, temp, atemp (feels-like temperature), humidity, windspeed, casual, registered, count
Target variable: count (sum of casual + registered rentals)
Datetime string: converted into month, dayofweek, hour
Our methodology followed three stages: feature engineering, model selection, and evaluation.
Based on insights from Du, He, and Zhechev (2014), we applied the following transformations:
Datetime decomposition: Split datetime into month, dayofweek, and hour, isolating the time-of-day signal.
Peak-hour indicator: Created a binary peak_hour feature:
Feature removal: Dropped holiday (no predictive signal per the paper) and temp (highly correlated with atemp, causing collinearity).
We trained and 10-fold cross-validated eight models across four categories:
CTree was approximated using scikit-learn's DecisionTreeRegressor, as the exact Conditional Inference Tree algorithm is available only in R's party package.

Following the reference paper, we also attempted split regression — training separate models on registered and casual counts and summing predictions — to test whether the two user groups respond differently to features.
The project was implemented in Python using pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn. The pipeline:
Apply feature engineering (decompose datetime, add peak-hour flag, drop unhelpful features)
Train each of the 8 models using 10-fold cross-validation
Compute mean CV RMSLE for each model
Select the best model, retrain on the full training set
Predict on the test set and save submission.csv
Visualize feature importances and model comparison
The RMSLE metric was implemented manually:

Tree-based models dominated. Split regression and Random Forest achieved the lowest CV RMSLE (0.3928 and 0.3985 respectively). The gap between them is within cross-validation noise, so they are effectively equivalent.
Time-of-day is the dominant signal. Feature importance analysis showed peak_hour (0.42) and hour (0.22) account for ~64% of the model's decision-making.
Weather plays a secondary role. atemp (0.14) and humidity (0.07) contribute meaningfully but are less predictive than time-of-day.
Linear models failed. Bike demand is highly non-linear (e.g., hour 8 AM ≠ 8× hour 1 AM), which linear models cannot capture. All three linear variants (Linear, PCR, GLMNet) had RMSLE > 1.16.
Stacking underperformed. Our base models (RF + CTree) were both tree-based, so they made similar errors. Stacking works best with diverse base models.

Split regression performed well. It slightly edged out direct count regression, though the difference is negligible. This contrasts with the reference paper, where split regression performed noticeably worse.

Tree-based models, particularly Random Forest and split regression, significantly outperformed linear and kernel approaches for this problem. Our best models achieved a CV RMSLE of 0.3928, beating the reference paper's benchmark of 0.503. The most predictive feature was peak_hour, followed by hour and atemp — confirming that time-of-day patterns are the dominant driver of bike rental demand, with weather conditions playing a secondary but non-trivial role.
The 10-fold CV uses shuffled data, which mixes past and future observations. A time-series split would better reflect real-world deployment.
True CTree (via R's party package) may yield slightly different results than our DecisionTree substitute.
GLMNet with Poisson loss (rather than Gaussian) could improve the regularized linear model, since our target is a count variable.
Hyperparameter tuning for GBM could close the gap with Random Forest.
